response.title: The Ways To Wealth on Facebook: "📋 Federal rules at 42 CFR 422.2264 and 423.2264 prohibit Medicare plans and agents from making unsol…"
response.snippet:
An unsolicited Medicare plan sales call is a red flag: it could be a marketer violating CMS rules or a scammer trying to get your Medicare information.

Medicare itself will never call to sell you anything, and it does not call out of the blue asking you to "verify" your number.

There are legitimate calls, though: your own plan may contact you about coverage you already have, and an agent may call clients they already work with or anyone who gave permission.

Medicare Open Enrollment starts October 15 and runs through December 7, and these calls pick up right alongside it, so the line to remember is simple: a stranger pitching a plan you never asked about is never legitimate.

If you get one, hang up and report it by calling Medicare directly. [...] # The Ways To Wealth on Facebook: "📋 Federal rules at 42 CFR 422.2264 and 423.2264 prohibit Medicare plans and agents from making unsol…"

📋 Federal rules at 42 CFR 422.2264 and 423.2264 prohibit Medicare plans and agents from making unsolicited sales calls, texts, or door-to-door visits to anyone who has not given permission to be contacted.

That means the stranger on the phone offering a "free plan review" is breaking the rules before they say a second sentence.

What plans and agents can legally send without permission is postal mail and email with an opt-out, which is why your mailbox fills up every fall but your phone should stay quiet.

# The Ways To Wealth on Facebook: "📋 Federal rules at 42 CFR 422.2264 and 423.2264 prohibit Medicare plans and agents from making unsol…"

📋 Federal rules at 42 CFR 422.2264 and 423.2264 prohibit Medicare plans and agents from making unsolicited sales calls, texts, or door-to-door visits to anyone who has not given permission to be contacted.

That means the stranger on the phone offering a "free plan review" is breaking the rules before they say a second sentence.

What plans and agents can legally send without permission is postal mail and email with an opt-out, which is why your mailbox fills up every fall but your phone should stay quiet.

An unsolicited Medicare plan sales call is a red flag: it could be a marketer violating CMS rules or a scammer trying to get your Medicare information.

Medicare itself will never call to sell you anything, and it does not call out of the blue asking you to "verify" your number.

There are legitimate calls, though: your own plan may contact you about coverage you already have, and an agent may call clients they already work with or anyone who gave permission.

Medicare Open Enrollment starts October 15 and runs through December 7, and these calls pick up right alongside it, so the line to remember is simple: a stranger pitching a plan you never asked about is never legitimate.

If you get one, hang up and report it by calling Medicare directly.

Has anyone in your family gotten one of these "plan review" calls?

response.title: Medicare fraud and scams: How to spot them and protect yourself | medicareresources.org
response.snippet:
Legitimate Medicare plans do not pressure people into immediate decisions or request sensitive information during unexpected calls.13 In fact, Medicare Advantage plans are not allowed to make unsolicited phone calls to prospective members. They can only call if you’re already enrolled, requested contact, or called them first.13 If your plan is ending or changing, you’ll receive official written notice from your current plan or Medicare. Licensed agents can help you compare plans, but you should never feel rushed into switching.

#### Free medical equipment scams [...] Stay informed about current scams. Monitor consumer alerts from the Office of Inspector General to learn about the latest fraud schemes targeting Medicare beneficiaries.27
   Add your phone number to the National Do Not Call Registry. Register at gov or call 1-888-382-1222. While this won’t stop all unwanted calls, it can reduce them.
   Be extra cautious during Medicare Open Enrollment. Scam activity increases during this period, so only work with licensed insurance agents you have contacted yourself.
   Know how Medicare communicates. Medicare primarily sends information by mail. They won’t call you to ask for personal information unless you contacted them first, and they won’t threaten to cancel your coverage. [...] Red flags to note:12

   Unsolicited calls pressuring you to switch plans
   Claims that your current plan is ending when you haven’t received official written notice from your plan
   Promises of benefits that sound too good to be true
   Requests for your Medicare number to check your eligibility before explaining plan details

# Medicare fraud and scams: How to spot them and protect yourself

## Learn to recognize the most common Medicare fraud schemes and scams, and what to do if you’ve been targeted.

Author: [Maggie Aime](https://www.medicareresources.org/authors/maggie-aime/) | Date Posted: January 26, 2026

![Image 8: hero-image](https://www.medicareresources.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/medicare-fraud-scams-700x355.webp)

### In this article

*   [Medicare fraud vs. Medicare scams: What’s the difference?](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#difference)
*   [What are the most common types of Medicare fraud?](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#fraud)
*   [What are the most common types of Medicare scams?](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#scams)
*   [I gave my Medicare number to a scammer, now what?](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#number)
*   [How can I protect myself from Medicare fraud and scams?](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#protect)

Medicare loses an estimated $60 billion each year due to fraud and scams.[1](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_1_76946 "“Dollars Lost to Fraud” Senior Medicare Patrol. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") In Fiscal Year 2024 alone, Medicare paid out $31.70 billion in improper payments, which include fraud, waste, and abuse.[2](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_2_76946 "“Fiscal Year 2024 Improper Payments Fact Sheet” CMS.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

Healthcare scams cost consumers $17 million in losses in 2023, although the actual figure is estimated to be much higher, as these losses aren’t always reported.[3](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_3_76946 "“2024 Fighting Fraud: Scams to Watch Out For” page 55. U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") Health-related scams tend to spike during Medicare Open Enrollment[4](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_4_76946 "“Medicare.gov. Accessed Jan. 14, 2026") ([October 15 to December 7](https://www.medicareresources.org/medicare-open-enrollment/)), when scammers take advantage of consumer confusion and time pressure.[3](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_3_76946 "“2024 Fighting Fraud: Scams to Watch Out For” page 55. U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

Healthcare fraud and scams are not the same thing, though both can leave enrollees dealing with financial loss, stress, and hours spent fixing the damage.[5](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_5_76946 "“Medicare Fraud & Abuse: Prevent, Detect, Report” page 6. CMS.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")[6](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_6_76946 "“Older Americans and Medicare Call Scams” FCC.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") Here’s the difference between Medicare fraud and Medicare scams, how to protect yourself, and what to do if you think you’ve been targeted.  
[](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/)

### Medicare fraud vs. Medicare scams: What’s the difference?

Medicare fraud occurs when someone knowingly and incorrectly bills Medicare for services or supplies, to receive unauthorized benefits or payment.[5](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_5_76946 "“Medicare Fraud & Abuse: Prevent, Detect, Report” page 6. CMS.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") The majority of fraud activity is done by healthcare providers, medical suppliers, or insurance brokers, although enrollees may commit healthcare fraud in rare situations.[7](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_7_76946 "“Health Care Fraud” FBI.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

Though these types of fraud are committed against the Medicare program itself, they can affect enrollees through unexpected bills and denied coverage.

Medicare scams, on the other hand, directly target Medicare beneficiaries. Scammers often pose as Medicare representatives, health plans, or healthcare workers to trick consumers into divulging their Medicare ID, Social Security number, or bank information.[6](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_6_76946 "“Older Americans and Medicare Call Scams” FCC.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

Once scammers obtain this information, they may file fraudulent claims in the beneficiary’s name, which can lead to identity theft, billing issues, and problems with Medicare coverage.[8](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_8_76946 "“Fraud Schemes” Senior Medicare Patrol. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

![Image 9: Back to top](https://www.medicareresources.org/wp-content/themes/mro/assets/images/down-arrow.svg)

Back to top

  
[](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/)  

### What are the most common types of Medicare fraud?

While fraud schemes vary, they share a common goal: getting payments from Medicare by lying or overcharging. Common types of Medicare fraud include:[5](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_5_76946 "“Medicare Fraud & Abuse: Prevent, Detect, Report” page 6. CMS.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")[9](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_9_76946 "“Common Types of Health Care Fraud Fact Sheet” CMS.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

*   **Phantom billing:**Medicare is charged for doctor visits, tests, or equipment that never took place or were never delivered.
*   **Upcoding:** A provider charges for a more expensive procedure or service than what was rendered.
*   **Unbundling:** Services that should be billed together at a lower cost are split into separate charges to increase payment.
*   **Double-billing:** A service or supply is inappropriately billed to Medicare more than once.
*   **Unnecessary services:** A provider performs and bills for tests, treatments, or supplies that aren’t medically needed.
*   **Kickbacks:** Providers receive money or other incentives in exchange for referring patients for tests, treatments, or services.
*   **“Free” offers:** Providers advertise “free” medical equipment or services to beneficiaries but bill Medicare without the beneficiary’s knowledge or consent.
*   **Medical identity theft:** Someone uses another beneficiary’s Medicare number to receive care or bill services fraudulently.

![Image 10: Back to top](https://www.medicareresources.org/wp-content/themes/mro/assets/images/down-arrow.svg)

Back to top

  
[](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/)  

### What are the most common types of Medicare scams?

Medicare scams tend to follow a pattern: they create urgency, sound official, and pressure people to act quickly before there’s time to double-check the details. These schemes don’t come from Medicare itself. They come from criminals who are attempting to steal personal information or money.[6](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_6_76946 "“Older Americans and Medicare Call Scams” FCC.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

Below are some of the most common Medicare scams, how they work, and how to spot them:

#### Calls or messages asking to verify Medicare information

In this common scam, a Medicare beneficiary receives a call, text, or email claiming that Medicare needs to verify their identity to prevent the beneficiary’s benefits from being suspended or canceled.[6](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_6_76946 "“Older Americans and Medicare Call Scams” FCC.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") Scammers often use threatening language like “Your account has been flagged for suspicious activity” or “You’ll lose your coverage if you don’t act immediately.”[6](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_6_76946 "“Older Americans and Medicare Call Scams” FCC.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

**Red flags to note:**[10](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_10_76946 "“Protect Yourself from Social Security Scams” SSA.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

*   Requests for Medicare or Social Security numbers
*   Urgent deadlines or threats of coverage loss
*   Claims that the caller is “from Medicare” without you contacting them first

Medicare and Social Security Administration representatives will never contact you to ask for your personal information, such as your Social Security, bank account, or your Medicare identification number.[11](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_11_76946 "“Your Medicare Card” Medicare.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

But if you call Medicare or the Social Security Administration and ask the representative to access your account, you’ll be asked for your Medicare or Social Security number.[11](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_11_76946 "“Your Medicare Card” Medicare.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") In this case, you’ve initiated the call yourself to these official entities, so you can feel confident providing the information they request.

Beware of spoofing, a technology scammers often use to manipulate caller ID information to make a call look like it’s coming from a government agency or a familiar healthcare provider.[6](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_6_76946 "“Older Americans and Medicare Call Scams” FCC.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") If you receive an unexpected call asking for personal information, hang up. After hanging up, you can always call Medicare directly at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to verify whether a call is legitimate.

#### Open enrollment plan-switching scams

Scammers often take advantage of the Medicare Open Enrollment period to pose as insurance agents or plan representatives. They often use high-pressure tactics, claiming a beneficiary’s current plan is being discontinued or that they need to switch immediately to avoid losing coverage.[6](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_6_76946 "“Older Americans and Medicare Call Scams” FCC.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

Scammers may also promise benefits that don’t exist or misrepresent what a plan covers. Their goal is to earn a commission from enrolling you in a new plan without clear consent.

**Red flags to note:**[12](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_12_76946 "“Older Americans and Medicare Call Scams | Federal Communications Commission” FCC.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

*   Unsolicited calls pressuring you to switch plans
*   Claims that your current plan is ending when you haven’t received official written notice from your plan
*   Promises of benefits that sound too good to be true
*   Requests for your Medicare number to check your eligibility before explaining plan details

Legitimate Medicare plans do not pressure people into immediate decisions or request sensitive information during unexpected calls.[13](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_13_76946 "“eCFR: 42 CFR 422.2264 – Beneficiary contact” ECFR.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") In fact, [Medicare Advantage](https://www.medicare.gov/health-drug-plans/health-plans) plans are not allowed to make unsolicited phone calls to prospective members. They can only call if you’re already enrolled, requested contact, or called them first.[13](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_13_76946 "“eCFR: 42 CFR 422.2264 – Beneficiary contact” ECFR.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") If your plan is ending or changing, you’ll receive official written notice from your current plan or Medicare. Licensed agents can help you compare plans, but you should never feel rushed into switching.

#### Free medical equipment scams

Another common scam involves offers for “free” medical equipment, such as back braces, orthotics, or urinary catheters, with scammers claiming Medicare approved the item or that a healthcare provider recommended it.[14](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_14_76946 "“Consumer Alert: Urinary Catheter Scams” OIG.HHS.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") They’ll generally ask for your Medicare number, then turn around and bill Medicare for equipment that was never needed, approved, or delivered.[15](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_15_76946 "“Durable Medical Equipment Fraud” Senior Medicare Patrol. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

**Red flags to note:**[15](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_15_76946 "“Durable Medical Equipment Fraud” Senior Medicare Patrol. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

*   Unsolicited calls, texts, or door-to-door visits offering “free” equipment
*   Claims that equipment is “completely covered by Medicare” without a doctor’s order
*   Pressure to provide your Medicare number immediately to verify eligibility
*   Equipment arrives that you didn’t request

[Medicare covers durable medical equipment](https://www.medicareresources.org/faqs/does-medicare-cover-durable-medical-equipment-dme/) only when it’s medically necessary and ordered by your doctor.[16](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_16_76946 "“Durable Medical Equipment Coverage” Medicare.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") If you didn’t discuss it with your healthcare provider, it’s a scam.

#### Free genetic or at-home testing scams

You might receive phone calls, mailers, or ads promoting “free” genetic tests or at-home testing kits for cancer screening, dementia detection, heart disease, or medication metabolism testing.[17](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_17_76946 "“Genetic Testing Fraud” Senior Medicare Patrol. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") Some scammers set up booths at community events, health fairs, or senior centers, offering free cheek swab tests.[18](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_18_76946 "“Beware of a Growing Medicare Scam: “Free Genetic Testing” Senior Medicare Patrol. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") Once they obtain your Medicare number, they bill Medicare thousands of dollars for tests that weren’t medically necessary or ordered by your doctor.[18](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_18_76946 "“Beware of a Growing Medicare Scam: “Free Genetic Testing” Senior Medicare Patrol. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

**Red flags to note:**[18](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_18_76946 "“Beware of a Growing Medicare Scam: “Free Genetic Testing” Senior Medicare Patrol. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

*   Offers for “free” genetic or cardiovascular testing without your doctor’s order
*   Genetic testing offered at health fairs, senior centers, parking lots, or through unsolicited calls where you’re requested to provide your Medicare information
*   Use of telemedicine where a healthcare provider you’ve never met orders the test
*   Testing kits arrive that you didn’t request
*   Charges on your Medicare Summary Notice (MSN) for Original Medicare beneficiaries, or explanation of benefits (EOB) for Medicare Advantage enrollees, for expensive genetic tests you don’t remember receiving

Medicare covers genetic testing for certain cancer risks or to determine how a person may respond to medications, but only when medically necessary and ordered by a qualified healthcare professional.[19](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_19_76946 "“LCD – BRCA1 and BRCA2 Genetic Testing (L36715)” CMS.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")[20](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_20_76946 "“LCD – Pharmacogenomics Testing (L39073)” CMS.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") Legitimate genetic tests aren’t offered for free at public events or through random phone calls.

#### Medicare data breach scams

When a real [data breach affecting Medicare beneficiaries](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/was-your-medicare-data-affected-by-a-data-breach/) is announced in the news, scammers jump on the opportunity to get the information. They contact people claiming to be from Medicare or a related agency, saying they need to verify information or issue new identification numbers due to the breach.[21](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_21_76946 "“Monitor Breaches and Watch for Scams” Privacy.ca.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") These scams resurface every time a healthcare data breach makes headlines.

**Red flags to note:**[21](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_21_76946 "“Monitor Breaches and Watch for Scams” Privacy.ca.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

*   Calls or texts referencing a recent data breach you heard about in the news
*   Claims you need to “protect your account” or “verify your information” immediately
*   Requests for your Medicare number, Social Security number, or bank information
*   Pressure to act quickly to get a new card or avoid losing coverage

If a data breach affects your Medicare information, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services will mail you a letter. The letter will explain what happened, what information was compromised, and steps you should take, if any.[22](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_22_76946 "“CMS Notifies Individuals Potentially Impacted by Data Incident” CMS.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") Medicare will never contact you by phone, email, or text to ask for your personal information or tell you to get a new card due to a breach.

### I gave my Medicare number to a scammer, now what?

If you shared your Medicare number and later felt there was something suspicious about your interaction, it’s understandable to feel worried and upset, but taking action quickly can help mitigate the damage and protect your benefits. Here’s what to do:[23](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_23_76946 "“Reporting Medicare Fraud & Abuse” Medicare.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

*   **Call Medicare immediately at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).** Let them know your Medicare number may have been compromised. They can flag your account and give you guidance on the next steps.
*   **Carefully review your Medicare Summary Notice (or explanation of benefits, if you’re on Medicare Advantage).** Check for charges for services, tests, or equipment that don’t look familiar or were never received.[24](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_24_76946 "“Medicare Summary Notice (MSN)” Medicare.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")
*   **Report any suspicious charges.**Contact Medicare right away to notify them of any unfamiliar charges so they can investigate and stop future payments.
*   **Request a new Medicare card if needed.** If you believe your Medicare number is being misused, you can request a replacement card through your [gov](http://medicare.gov/) account or by calling Medicare.[11](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_11_76946 "“Your Medicare Card” Medicare.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")
*   **Place a fraud alert with the credit bureaus if your Social Security number was also compromised.** Contact Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion to add a fraud alert to your credit report.[25](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_25_76946 "“Credit Freezes and Fraud Alerts” Consumer.FTC.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025") Also, report the crime to the Federal Trade Commission online at [gov](https://identitytheft.gov/) or by calling 1-877-IDTHEFT (1-877-438-4338).
*   **Report the scam to the Office of Inspector General (OIG).** Call the fraud hotline at 1-800-HHS-TIPS (1-800-447-8477) or [file a report online](https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/report-fraud/).

### How can I protect myself from Medicare fraud and scams?

The best way to avoid becoming a victim is to stay alert to red flags and guard your information. Consider the following steps:[26](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_26_76946 "“Medicare Scams: How to Protect Yourself” National Council on Aging. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")

*   **Treat your Medicare number like a credit card.** Never share your Medicare or Social Security number with anyone who contacts you unexpectedly. Your Medicare information should only be shared directly with your healthcare provider’s office or during calls and appointments you schedule. Any other request should raise concern.
*   **Hang up on unexpected calls that ask for personal information.** If the call claims to be from Medicare, Social Security, or a health plan, call back using the entity’s official phone number. Scammers can make a call appear to come from an official agency, clinic, or plan, so don’t trust caller ID alone. If something feels off about the call, trust your instincts and hang up.
*   **Review claims regularly.** Check the Medicare Summary Notice (for Original Medicare) or Explanation of Benefits (for Medicare Advantage and Part D plans). Report any charges that do not make sense.
*   **Track your care.** Keep a list of appointments, tests, and equipment received so it is easier to identify false claims.
*   **Use a Medicare account to monitor activity.** Set up access at [gov](http://mymedicare.gov/) to view claims and catch issues sooner.
*   **Don’t click on links in suspicious emails or text messages.** Scammers create fake emails and texts that appear to come from Medicare. Never click links or open attachments from unsolicited messages. If you need to access your Medicare account, type Medicare.gov directly into your browser.
*   **Stay informed about current scams.** Monitor [consumer alerts from the Office of Inspector General](https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/consumer-alerts/) to learn about the latest fraud schemes targeting Medicare beneficiaries.[27](https://www.medicareresources.org/blog/medicare-fraud-and-scams-how-to-spot-them-and-protect-yourself/#footnote_27_76946 "“Consumer Alerts” OIG.HHS.gov. Accessed Dec. 20, 2025")
*   **Add your phone number to the National Do Not Call Registry.** Register at [gov](https://donotcall.gov/) or call 1-888-382-1222. While this won’t stop all unwanted calls, it can reduce them.
*   **Be extra cautious during Medicare Open Enrollment.** Scam activity increases during this period, so only work with licensed insurance agents you have contacted yourself.
*   **Know how Medicare communicates.** Medicare primarily sends information by mail. They won’t call you to ask for personal information unless you contacted them first, and they won’t threaten to cancel your coverage.
*   **Shred documents with personal information.** Before throwing away documents that contain personally identifiable information (PII) or protected health information (PHI), shred them.
*   **Limit what gets shared publicly.** Avoid posting birthdate, address, or insurance details on social media. Scammers can use these small details to sound convincing.
*   **Be skeptical of too good to be true offers.** Free equipment or promises of extra benefits in exchange for your Medicare number are red flags.

If you’re unsure about a phone call, hang up and call them directly at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).

# 5 Warning Signs of a Medicare Scam—and How to Protect Yourself

[Medicare](/older-adults/benefits/healthcare/medicare/)

10 min read

## Related Topics

* [Health Care Benefits](/older-adults/benefits/healthcare/)
* [Medicare](/older-adults/benefits/healthcare/medicare/)

You can encounter a [Medicare](/article/what-is-medicare-and-how-do-i-get-started/) scam by phone, email, text, social media—or even at your front door. Whether scammers pretend to represent Medicare, an insurance company, or a doctor’s office, their goal is the same: to get their hands on your Medicare number and other personal information and use it for their own personal gain.

Knowing the warning signs of a Medicare scam can help you stop fraud before it happens.

## 5 Warning Signs of a Medicare Scam

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Warning sign** | **What to watch for** |
| **Promises of free items or services** | Offers for "free" medical equipment, prescriptions, genetic tests, or screenings in exchange for your Medicare number |
| **Pressure to switch plans** | Claims that you're pre-approved for a better plan or must pay a fee to enroll |
| **Requests to update your Medicare card** | Calls saying you must activate, renew, or upgrade your card by providing personal information or paying a fee |
| **Threats to cancel your coverage** | Warnings that you'll lose your benefits unless you verify information or change plans immediately |
| **Claims that you're owed a "refund"** | Requests for your Medicare number or banking information so you can supposedly receive money |

Below, learn about these five common red flags, what to do if something doesn’t seem right, and how to protect your personal information.

## What is a Medicare scam?

“In a [Medicare scam](https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2024/11/avoid-scams-during-medicares-open-enrollment-period), one or more criminals pretend to be from Medicare or another known organization. Their goal is to trick benficiaries into sharing their Medicare or Social Security number (or in some cases, making a payment). Most often, scammers use this information to commit identity theft. They submit bogus Medicare claims in the beneficiary’s name to obtain health care services, supplies, or even prescription drugs.

Earlier this year, a former California teacher pleaded guilty to helping carry out a [$51 million Medicare fraud scheme](https://www.medicaleconomics.com/view/teacher-pleads-guilty-in-51m-medicare-fraud-scheme-cms-to-ask-states-to-revalidate-high-risk-medicaid-providers-ai-model-predicts-cancer-survival-from-single-cell-tumor-model-morning-medical-update) involving orthotic braces beneficiaries did not request or use. The group submitted fraudulent claims using fake prescriptions and received about $20 million from Medicare. The teacher admitted to helping launder at least $14 million and paying $3.7 million in kickbacks to sham marketing companies.

Sadly, this is just the tip of the iceberg. Senior Medicare Patrol estimates that fraud, errors, and abuse cost Medicare about $60 billion each year, although the true amount is difficult to determine.**1**

“Medicare scams are tough to detect as they’re happening, so the true cost is probably much higher,” said Ryan Ramsey, Associate Director of Health Care and Benefits at NCOA. “And Medicare isn’t the only one that pays the price. Older adults whose Medicare numbers are stolen may face copayments or reach coverage limits for services they never received.”

Fraudulent claims can also become part of a person’s Medicare record. This may make it harder for health care providers to see an accurate picture of the patient’s medical history and determine what care they really need.

## What are the most common Medicare scams?

For instance, someone may call you offering a “free” medical device, or ask you to confirm your Medicare number. They may even threaten to terminate your Medicare benefits. When they get your personal information, they use it to bill Medicare for services or supplies you never received, or they may steal your identity entirely to commit other crimes (identity theft).

Medicare scammers often use the phone to find their targets, but they may also reach out via email, text messages, and postal mail. They may pose as Medicare representatives, health care providers, medical supply vendors, or insurance agents. “The tricky part is that scammers can sound very professional and persuasive over the phone,” Ramsey explained. “Increasingly, they also use technology like AI to create convincing websites, emails, and print materials that appear to be from trustworthy organizations.”

Learning all you can about Medicare scams can help you stay one step ahead of these criminals.

## What are the warning signs of a Medicare scam?

Look out for these red flags to keep yourself and others safe:

1. **Promises of free items or services:** Be suspicious of any offers involving no-cost medical supplies, medical care, or prescription medications. Many scammers will offer older adults valuable medical equipment, persuade them to share their Medicare number, and then use that information to file high-cost Medicare claims in the beneficiary’s name. Also, beware of offers for free genetic testing or screenings that were not ordered by your physician. This is a [known Medicare scam](https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/consumer-alerts/fraud-alert-genetic-testing-scam/).
2. **Pressure to switch your Medicare plan:** A scammer, often claiming to be from Medicare, may say you're “pre-approved” for a new health care plan or drug plan with lower premiums or better benefits. They may tell you there’s a fee to enroll in this new plan.
3. **Notices to renew or upgrade your Medicare card:** A fraudster may call and say you need to activate, renew, or upgrade your Medicare card. They may ask for your Medicare number to “verify” your account, or they may request that you pay a processing fee.
4. **Threats to cancel your coverage:** You may receive a call stating there’s a problem with your Medicare account, such as fraudulent activity. The caller says your benefits will be canceled if you don’t immediately verify your personal information or join a new plan.
5. **Claims you’re eligible for a refund:** Another common Medicare scam tactic is telling older adults they qualify for a refund due to changes in their plan. The scammer may ask for your Medicare number—and even your bank account details.

## How can I protect myself from Medicare scams?

Scammers are everywhere, and [Medicare scams](https://www.cnbc.com/2022/07/21/medicare-scams-are-on-the-rise-here-are-four-tips-to-avoid-them.html) can happen to anyone. The tips below can help you keep your personal information safe.

* **Avoid sharing your Medicare number with people who contact you out of the blue:** Do not provide your Medicare card, Medicare number, Social Security card, or Social Security number to anyone but your doctor, pharmacy, or people who work with Medicare to assist beneficiaries. Protect these numbers just like you would protect your credit card, debit card, or bank account information. It’s important to know that Medicare will not call you unless you’ve specifically asked for help. And if they do call you in response to a request, they will not need your information since they’ll already have it on file.  
     
   Does your caller ID show a legitimate-looking phone number? Don’t be fooled. Scammers can spoof (or fake) their number to make it look like the call is coming from a government agency or other known organization. Also, don’t be surprised if the caller has some basic information about you. With the internet, those details are easy to find today. If someone unfamiliar calls asking you for personal details, simply hang up.
* **Be wary of Facebook Medicare ads:** [Misleading Medicare ads](https://www.aol.com/articles/report-shows-costly-medicare-scams-191300000.html) that may be designed to steal your personal information are rampant on this popular social media platform. According to watchdog group the Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH), Medicare scam ads on Facebook received more than 215 million views in the past year, nearly six times the number recorded in all previous years combined. Current tactics include politically branded ads featuring phony Medicare plan endorsements from well-known politicians. [Other ads targeting older adults](https://www.foxnews.com/tech/meta-medicare-scam-ads-targeting-seniors-face-scrutiny) offer thousands of dollars in "free benefits" through Medicare Advantage plans.
* **Do not click on suspicious links:** Criminals create fake email addresses to make it seem like their messages are coming directly from Medicare. These emails may send you to a website that looks authentic. Do not respond to unexpected emails or text messages or click on any links they contain—even if the communication looks real.  
     
   If you need to update your information, log in to your Medicare account at [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/), call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227), or talk to a trusted advisor.
* **Do not be afraid of threats to terminate benefits:** If you qualify for Medicare, your benefits will not be taken away for reasons scammers typically use, like not signing up for a certain plan.
* **Do not speak to anyone who tries to persuade you to choose a certain plan:** Ignore claims that any policy is “preferred by Medicare." This is not true. Medicare does not endorse a specific plan.
* **Destroy your old Medicare card:** Some scammers may claim you need to return your old card. They are lying to you. If you receive a new card from Medicare, destroy your old one immediately. Medicare does not need it. Cut it up with scissors or a shredder and start using your new one right away.
* **Protect your medical records:** Do not allow anyone but your doctor or other health care providers to review your personal medical information.
* **Do not accept unauthorized genetic testing kits:** If you receive a genetic testing kit in the mail, and your doctor didn't order it, refuse the delivery outright or return it to the sender.

## How do I report Medicare scams?

If you or someone you know is a victim of a Medicare scam, take action by reporting it:

* Call Medicare directly at 1-800-MEDICARE (800-633-4227).
* Contact the Senior Medicare Patrol Resource Center by calling 1-877-808-2468 or use their [online contact form](https://www.smpresource.org/Contact/Default.aspx).
* [Submit a report online](https://ReportFraud.ftc.gov/#/?orgcode=NCOA) to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).

## Frequently asked questions (FAQ)

**Do Medicare scams increase during Open Enrollment?**  
   
 Yes. Fraudulent activity tends to ramp up during the yearly [Medicare Open Enrollment Period](/article/a-complete-guide-to-medicare-open-enrollment/) (Oct. 15 - Dec. 7), when beneficiaries are encouraged to review their health care coverage and make any necessary changes.

**Does Medicare ever call you?**

Rarely. Medicare may call you in limited situations, such as returning a call or following up on a request you made. But Medicare will not call out of the blue to sell you something, threaten to cancel your benefits, or ask for your Medicare number or other personal information. If you’re unsure about a phone call, hang up and call them directly at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).

**What can a scammer do with your Medicare number?**

A scammer can use your Medicare number to bill Medicare for medical care, equipment, tests, or supplies you never received. This can lead to fraudulent charges and inaccurate information in your medical records. You may even have trouble getting services you need that Medicare has already been (fraudulently) billed for.

**How can you tell whether a Medicare call is legitimate?**

Be suspicious if an unexpected caller asks for your Medicare number, Social Security number, banking information, or payment. Other warning signs include threats, pressure to act immediately, promises of “free” medical products, or claims you need a new Medicare card. When in doubt, hang up and contact Medicare directly using the number on your Medicare card.

**How can you get unbiased Medicare advice?**

Medicare enrollment choices can be tough to make—and if you don't take time to ensure you’re not overpaying or missing out on important services, it could cost you. That's where your [State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP)](/article/what-is-a-state-health-insurance-assistance-program-and-how-can-it-help-me/) can help. These organizations offer expert, unbiased counseling to Medicare-eligible people as well as their families and caregivers. Best of all, this service is 100% free. [Find your local SHIP now](https://www.shiphelp.org/).

### Source

1.  Senior Medicare Patrol. Medicare Fraud Prevention Week. June 2026. Found on the internet at https://smpresource.org/mfpw/medicare-fraud-prevention-week/

response.snippet:
Offers of new or upgraded cards for a fee. Medicare cards are paper; there are no plastic Medicare cards or chip-enabled cards. You can print a new Medicare card anytime from your online Medicare account. “No one would receive a new Medicare card unless they personally requested one from Medicare, like in a case where their ID has been compromised,” McKenna notes.

Requests for personal information. “Medicare will not call beneficiaries to ask for personal information or to update your information or give you a new Medicare card number,” says Rose Morales, an SMP fraud investigative analyst with California Health Advocates. [...] The ITRC also advises watching out for:

Offers of free equipment, screenings or services in exchange for your Medicare number.

Pressure to switch Medicare plans, especially with promises of unusually low premiums.

1. Know how Medicare works. As noted above, Medicare won’t call you out of the blue with requests for information or new card offers. Find out more at AARP’s Medicare resource center.

Medicare has been a favorite target of scammers from virtually the moment the program was signed into law in July 1965. And a favorite time for criminals to perpetrate their scams is during the open enrollment period, when enrollees can make changes to their plans — from October 15 through December 7.

You may, for example, receive a phone call from someone claiming to be with Medicare. They may know your personal details, like your date of birth or address. Don’t let that convince you the caller is legitimate; scammers can easily purchase or obtain such data. (The Federal Communications Commission offers audio clips demonstrating what these scam calls sound like.)

Unfortunately, many people don’t realize that Medicare won’t contact you out of the blue. Victims engage with these criminals, sometimes giving away personal financial information and Medicare details.

Criminals can then use that personal information to commit identity fraud (stealing money from victims’ bank accounts, among other potential fraud crimes). They might use the stolen Medicare number to make bogus claims, typically for medical equipment, genetic testing kits, diabetic supplies or deceptive hospice enrollments.

“Your Medicare number is as valuable to a criminal as your Social Security number,” says Eva Velasquez, CEO of the Identity Theft Resource Center. “Guard it accordingly.”

Some criminals who defraud Medicare can also cause unexpected harm to patients. Mike Cohen, the headquarters operations officer at the Office of Inspector General, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), says there are cases in which perpetrators bill Medicare in patients’ names for certain equipment, such as wheelchairs, or for lab tests that are a “lifetime” benefit. That means you only get the item or service once. And if that one opportunity is squandered due to fraud, the benefit is no longer available when the beneficiary actually needs it later.

Fraud, along with errors and abuse, causes Medicare to lose an estimated $60 billion annually — although, as the Senior Medicare Patrol notes, the exact figure is impossible to measure.

**New card offers.** Criminals pretend to be from Medicare and tell beneficiaries that they will receive a new Medicare card with a chip or one that is plastic instead of paper. (Medicare cards are paper and none have a chip.) They may even say the new card includes additional benefits, such as a gift card.

“The scammer will say they need to confirm the Medicare ID and other personal information. In some cases, they tell the person they just need to provide banking account information to make sure they can continue paying their premiums,” says Kim McKenna, Senior Medicare Patrol (SMP) coordinator for the Washington State Office of the Insurance Commissioner.

**Submission of false claims.** “\[Criminals] may use a person’s ID to contact a doctor’s office and request an order for medical equipment or tests, then submit claims without the beneficiary even knowing,” McKenna says. Scammers then get reimbursed by Medicare for the fake services.

Criminals take advantage of the fact that Medicare beneficiaries typically don’t receive a bill if Medicare and a supplemental policy cover the full cost, so victims may not even become aware of the fraud until services they didn’t receive appear on their quarterly summary notice.

This can result in hundreds of millions in fraudulent claims, with one recent case involving $644 million in billed charges. Criminals often use the stolen Medicare provider numbers of legitimate physicians to authorize these claims without their knowledge.

**Free genetic testing scams.** These have become increasingly common, according to Velasquez: Someone contacts you offering a free genetic screening, then collects your Medicare number and bills Medicare for tests that were never ordered by your physician and may never have been performed.”

Here’s what you can do to help protect people 50 and older from scams and fraud:

**Free “MyChart Medicare Kit.”** Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday was among a long list of health care organizations that recently warned that scammers were impersonating MyChart (a patient portal used by many health care providers) and sending messages offering a “MyChart Medicare Kit,” a fictional product. Sunday said it’s a way to get recipients to click malicious links, allowing hackers to access patients’ MyChart portals.

**Unexpected calls from someone claiming to work for Medicare.** “The only time someone would receive a call from Medicare is if the beneficiary called Medicare first and scheduled a phone appointment with a representative,” McKenna says.

**Offers of new or upgraded cards for a fee.** Medicare cards are paper; there are no plastic Medicare cards or chip-enabled cards. You can print a new Medicare card anytime from your online Medicare account. “No one would receive a new Medicare card unless they personally requested one from Medicare, like in a case where their ID has been compromised,” McKenna notes.

**Requests for personal information.** “Medicare will not call beneficiaries to ask for personal information or to update your information or give you a new Medicare card number,” says Rose Morales, an SMP fraud investigative analyst with California Health Advocates.

**Callers who don’t clearly identify themselves.** “Most scammers use generic phrases like ‘I’m calling from your health care provider’ or ‘I’m calling from Medicare Services,’ ” Morales says.

**Threats of coverage cancellation.** The caller says they’ll cancel your Medicare coverage unless you provide personal information over the phone. Medicare will never call you about canceling your coverage, and you will receive several bills and a delinquency notice in the mail before Medicare cancels your coverage for not paying Part B premiums.

**Strange bills or charges.** Take note if you receive a bill from a hospital or medical provider for care you didn’t receive, or you see a suspicious charge on your Medicare summary notice, which is your quarterly explanation of benefits from Medicare.

The ITRC also advises watching out for:

Offers of free equipment, screenings or services in exchange for your Medicare number.

Pressure to switch Medicare plans, especially with promises of unusually low premiums.

**1. Know how Medicare works.** As noted above, Medicare won’t call you out of the blue with requests for information or new card offers. Find out more at AARP’s Medicare resource center.

**2. Hang up immediately.** If someone asks for your Medicare card number, hang up and call back using the number you know is associated with them. Don’t use a number they give you. (It’s good practice to never answer calls from people you don’t know.)

**3. Don’t join a Medicare health or drug plan over the phone** unless you called and asked for help; Medicare.gov advises.

**4. Keep your Medicare card at home.** Only carry your Medicare card if you need it for a medical appointment. If you’re worried about what happens if you’re in an accident, you can keep a copy of the card in your wallet with the number crossed out. If you’re in an accident, you’ll only need to show that you have Medicare and your coverage start date; you can provide the number later.

**5. Read your Medicare claims notices.** Look for claims for services you didn’t receive or for duplicate claims. You can check your claims record by reviewing the notice you receive in the mail every three months, or you can sign up to receive monthly electronic statements. To see current claims, go to your online Medicare account.

**6. Investigate odd charges.** If you find suspicious charges on your Medicare summary notice, first contact your doctor’s office to ensure it isn’t just an error, and then contact Medicare or your local SMP to report the activity.

Report the call to Medicare at 800-633-4227 and your state’s Senior Medicare Patrol at 877-808-2468. SMP volunteers can answer questions about suspicious charges and potential scams and help you report the fraud to Medicare and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Inspector General, which investigates Medicare fraud. They can also help you determine whether your Medicare number has been compromised, and you should get a new one.

Report scams to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3).

For support and guidance, the trained fraud specialists at the free AARP Fraud Watch Network Helpline﻿, 877-908-3360, can share information on what to do next and how to avoid future scams. The AARP Fraud Watch Network also offers free online group support sessions.

Scam of the Day

# Medicare Card Suspended Text Scam: How to Stay Safe

If you get a text message saying your Medicare card has been “suspended” or “deactivated” and you need to call a number or click a link to fix it, delete it immediately — it is a scam. Medicare does not send unsolicited text messages about your card status, and no legitimate government agency will ever threaten to cut off your benefits unless you hand over personal information or payment on the spot. This particular trick is surging in 2026, and it is catching people off guard because it looks and sounds alarmingly official.

## What does the Medicare card suspended text scam look like?

The message usually arrives out of nowhere. It might say something like: *“ALERT: Your Medicare card has been suspended due to suspicious activity. Call 1-800-XXX-XXXX immediately to restore your coverage.”* Some versions include a link to a fake website dressed up with Medicare logos and official-looking colors. Others ask you to reply with your Medicare number to “verify your identity.”

The goal is always the same: get your Medicare Beneficiary Identifier (MBI) — that is the unique number on your red, white, and blue Medicare card — along with your date of birth, Social Security number, or bank details. With those pieces, a scammer can bill Medicare fraudulently in your name, open accounts, or sell your information on the dark web.

## How can you tell if a Medicare call or text is a scam?

The single most important thing to remember is this: **Medicare will never contact you first by phone, text, or email to ask for your personal information.** If Medicare needs to reach you, they do it by postal mail. Here are the other red flags that tell you something is wrong:

* **Urgency and threats.** Real government agencies do not tell you your benefits will end in 24 hours unless you act right now. Pressure is the scammer’s best friend.
* **Requests for your Medicare number.** Medicare already has it. They will never ask you to “confirm” it over the phone or by text.
* **Unfamiliar phone numbers or short codes.** Legitimate Medicare communications come from known addresses and numbers you can verify at Medicare.gov.
* **Links in texts.** Do not tap any link in an unexpected Medicare-related text. Even if the URL looks close to official, it may be a convincing fake.
* **Bad grammar or odd formatting.** Government agencies proofread their communications. Misspellings and strange punctuation are warning signs.

## What should seniors do if they receive this text?

First, do not panic — and do not respond. Here is a simple action plan:

1. **Delete the text.** Do not click any link, call any number listed in the message, or reply.
2. **Report it.** Forward the text to 7726 (that spells SPAM on your keypad), which sends it directly to your mobile carrier for investigation. You can also report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to the HHS Office of Inspector General at 1-800-HHS-TIPS.
3. **Check your Medicare account.** Log in to MyMedicare.gov or call the real Medicare helpline at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to confirm your account is perfectly fine — which it almost certainly is.
4. **Tell someone you trust.** Scammers count on embarrassment keeping victims quiet. Telling a family member or friend helps you process what happened and may protect others.

**Enjoying this? Subscribe to Scam of the Day — it's free.**

[Subscribe free →](https://scam-of-the-day-newsletter.beehiiv.com/subscribe)

## What should you do if you already gave a scammer your information?

If you shared your Medicare number, Social Security number, or any financial details, move quickly — but know that acting fast can limit the damage.

* **Call Medicare immediately** at 1-800-633-4227 and report that your information was compromised. Ask them to flag your account for suspicious activity.
* **Contact the Social Security Administration** at 1-800-772-1213 if your Social Security number was shared.
* **Place a fraud alert or credit freeze** with all three credit bureaus — Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. A freeze is free and stops anyone from opening new credit in your name.
* **Monitor your Medicare Summary Notice** (the statement Medicare mails every three months) for any services billed that you never received.
* **File a police report** with your local department. This creates an official record that can help if you need to dispute fraudulent charges later.

You have not done anything wrong. These scams are sophisticated, and they are designed by professionals to trick smart, careful people.

## Why do scammers always ask for gift cards as payment?

You may have noticed that many scams — not just Medicare ones — eventually circle around to asking for payment in gift cards. There is a very practical reason scammers love them: gift cards are almost impossible to trace and cannot be reversed once the code is read out over the phone. Unlike a credit card charge or a wire transfer, there is no chargeback process. The moment you read those numbers aloud, the money is gone.

If anyone — claiming to be Medicare, the IRS, Social Security, or even a grandchild in trouble — ever asks you to pay a fine, fee, or debt using iTunes cards, Google Play cards, or any other gift card, that is a 100% guaranteed scam. No exceptions.

## How does the grandparent scam connect to Medicare fraud?

The grandparent scam is worth understanding here because scammers often run both plays at once, or switch between them if one stops working. In the grandparent scam, a caller pretends to be a grandchild (or a lawyer or police officer representing them) who is in urgent trouble — arrested, in a hospital, in an accident abroad — and needs money immediately. They beg you not to tell other family members.

The emotional manipulation is identical to the Medicare suspended text: urgency, secrecy, and fear. If you ever get a call like this, hang up and call your grandchild directly on a number you already have saved. Do not use any number the caller gives you.

Knowing how the grandparent scam works makes you better at spotting the Medicare version too, because the psychological machinery is the same. Scammers want you scared, rushed, and isolated. Slow down, and the illusion falls apart.

## Stay one step ahead — every single day

Scams evolve fast. The Medicare card suspended text is just today’s version of a trick that will look slightly different next week. The best protection is staying informed so the next scam feels familiar before it has a chance to fool you.

**Enjoying this? Subscribe to Scam of the Day — it's free.**

[Subscribe free →](https://scam-of-the-day-newsletter.beehiiv.com/subscribe)

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How can seniors spot a phone scam before it’s too late?**

The biggest warning signs are urgency, threats, and requests for personal information or payment. Legitimate government agencies like Medicare or the IRS will never demand immediate action over the phone or ask you to pay with gift cards. If something feels off, hang up and call the agency directly using a number from their official website.

**What should you do after giving a scammer your information?**

Act quickly: call Medicare at 1-800-633-4227 to flag your account, contact the Social Security Administration if your SSN was shared, and place a free credit freeze with all three major credit bureaus. Monitor your Medicare Summary Notice for services you never received, and file a report with the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

**How does the grandparent scam work and how do you stop it?**

A scammer calls pretending to be a grandchild — or someone helping them — claiming they’re in urgent trouble and need money immediately, usually asking you to keep it secret from other family members. To stop it, hang up and call your grandchild directly on a number you already have saved, and never wire money or buy gift cards based on an unexpected phone call.

**How can you tell if a Medicare call is a scam?**

Medicare will never call, text, or email you out of the blue to ask for your Medicare number or personal details — they already have that information and communicate by postal mail. Any message creating urgency around your benefits being suspended, or asking you to verify your Medicare Beneficiary Identifier (MBI) over the phone, is a scam.

**Why do scammers always ask for gift cards as payment?**

Gift cards are untraceable and irreversible — the moment you read the card number to a scammer, the money is gone with no way to get it back, unlike credit card charges which can be disputed. No real government agency, including Medicare, the IRS, or Social Security, will ever ask you to settle a debt or fine using gift cards.

Medicare and Social Security scams target older adults by impersonating trusted government programs and creating fear around benefits, medical coverage or legal trouble.

The scam may arrive as a phone call, text, email, social media ad or even a message that appears to come from a benefits office. The goal is usually simple: get sensitive information, redirect money or pressure someone into acting before they stop to verify the story.

These scams are effective because they sound official. A caller may claim your Medicare account needs to be verified, your Social Security number has been linked to fraud or your benefits are about to be suspended. In reality, that urgency is often the biggest warning sign.

Once people know the patterns, these schemes become much easier to spot and shut down. Here's how these scams work, the warning signs to watch for and the steps you can take to protect yourself or someone you love.

**IS ID.ME SAFE TO USE? WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW**

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers.

No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.

## How these scams usually work

Most Medicare and Social Security scams follow a familiar script. First, the scammer pretends to represent a trusted institution. Then he introduces a problem or opportunity — a frozen benefit, a replacement card, a refund, free medical equipment or a security issue tied to your identity. Finally, the sammer asks for personal details, payment information or immediate action.

A Medicare scam may ask for your Medicare number, Social Security number or bank details to "confirm" enrollment or process a benefit. A Social Security scam may claim your Social Security number has been suspended or linked to criminal activity and must be "reactivated" right away. These claims are false. Medicare does not cold-call people for sensitive information, and the Social Security Administration does not suspend Social Security numbers or demand instant payment to resolve a problem.

## Why seniors are a common target

Older adults are often singled out because scammers assume they are more likely to answer landlines, trust authority figures and have retirement savings or steady benefit income. Government impersonation scams are designed to exploit those assumptions with urgency, pressure and official-sounding language.

Scammers are also meeting seniors where they already spend time. Recent reporting has highlighted a surge in Medicare-related scam ads on Facebook, with roughly 73% of impressions from leading scam ads reaching users over 65. AI is making the problem worse too, with fraudsters using more polished scripts and, in some cases, cloned voices to sound more believable.

## Real examples of Medicare and Social Security scam tactics

One common Medicare scam offers free braces, genetic testing, screenings, grocery cards or other extra benefits in exchange for your Medicare number. Once scammers get that information, they may use it to bill Medicare fraudulently or as part of a larger identity theft scheme.

Another tactic plays on confusion about policy updates or refunds. A caller may say you overpaid for Medicare Part D, qualify for a refund or need to verify a new Medicare card. Then they ask for your Social Security number, bank account information or a fee to process the request. Legitimate agencies do not handle unexpected benefit issues this way.

Social Security scams usually rely on fear. A scammer may claim your Social Security number was used in a crime, your benefits are frozen or police will be contacted unless you verify your identity or send money immediately. Some scams even blend Medicare and Social Security language to sound more official.

**IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB?**

### Warning signs to watch for

The exact script changes, but the red flags are remarkably consistent.

### Unsolicited contact

An unexpected call, text or message claiming to be from Medicare or Social Security should always be treated carefully. Surprise outreach is a common trait of impersonation scams.

### Pressure to act right now

Scammers want people to feel rushed. They may say your benefits will end today, a refund will disappear or your identity is at immediate risk unless you comply.

### Requests for personal information

A request for your Medicare number, Social Security number, bank account details, passwords or one-time verification codes is a major red flag, especially during an unexpected contact.

### Demands for payment in unusual forms

Gift cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency, Zelle or cash-by-mail are strong signs of fraud. Government agencies do not demand payment that way.

### Threats or intimidation

If someone threatens arrest, benefit cancellation or legal action unless you act immediately, he is trying to trigger panic. That is not how legitimate agencies resolve problems.

### Caller ID that looks official

Scammers can spoof caller ID to display a local area code or names like Medicare or Social Security. A familiar-looking number is not proof that a call is real.

## 5 Prevention tips that actually help

The best defense is slowing the interaction down. A few simple habits can make it much harder for a scammer to catch you off guard.

### 1) Never share personal information unexpectedly

Never give out your Medicare number, Social Security number, bank details, passwords or verification codes during an unexpected call, text or message.

### 2) Verify the claim yourself

If someone claims to be from Medicare or Social Security, hang up and contact the agency yourself using the number on official mail, your card or the official website. Do not call a number provided by the person who contacted you.

### 3) Review your Medicare statements

Protect your Medicare number the same way you protect a credit card number. Review Medicare Summary Notices and Explanation of Benefits statements for services, equipment or providers you do not recognize.

### 4) Have a response ready

It helps to prepare a simple response before a suspicious call ever comes in. You can say, "I don't provide personal information over the phone. I'll call back using the official number." That gives you an easy way to end the conversation before a scammer can build more pressure.

### 5) How identity theft protection can add another layer of security

Medicare and Social Security scams can become far more damaging once a criminal gets your Social Security number, financial information or other personal details. That information can be used to open fraudulent accounts, take over existing accounts or commit identity theft long after the original scam call or message ends. Identity theft protection can add another layer of monitoring and support if that happens.

An identity theft protection service can combine identity and financial monitoring with alerts designed to help you spot suspicious activity sooner. Depending on the plan, monitoring may cover credit activity, financial accounts, investment and retirement accounts, phone takeovers, SIM swaps, utility accounts and other areas where criminals may try to use your identity.

What identity theft protection can help with:

- Identity recovery support: If your identity is stolen, a restoration specialist may be able to help guide you through the recovery process.
- Scam reimbursement: Some plans include reimbursement for certain eligible scam losses.
- Identity theft coverage: Higher-tier plans may include coverage for stolen funds, eligible personal expenses and legal or expert assistance following identity theft.
- Monitoring for suspicious activity: Alerts can help you investigate signs that someone may be using your identity or financial information without your permission.

Identity theft protection does not replace the precautions that can stop a Medicare or Social Security scam in the first place. You should still hang up on suspicious callers, independently verify benefit questions through official government channels and regularly review your Medicare and financial records. If you believe your Social Security number or other personal information has been compromised, act quickly.

Check whether your personal information may already be exposed

Scammers can be much more convincing when they already know details about you. A free exposure scan can help identify personal information connected to your email that may appear in known data breaches or on risky sites. Seeing what information may already be exposed can also help explain how a scammer knew enough about you to make a fake Medicare or Social Security message sound legitimate.

Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com

## What to do if you already responded

If you already shared personal or financial information, move quickly.

- Contact the relevant institution using its official number.
- Review bank and credit card activity for anything unfamiliar.
- Check Medicare records for claims you do not recognize.
- Consider a fraud alert or credit freeze if your Social Security number may have been exposed.
- Write down the date, phone number and details of the contact for your reports.

Quick action can reduce the odds of broader identity theft or financial damage.

## Kurt's key takeaways

Medicare and Social Security scams keep working because they target two things older Americans understandably take seriously: their health coverage and their financial security. What concerns me most is how much more convincing these scams are becoming. Criminals can combine personal information found online with spoofed phone numbers, polished messages and even AI-generated voices to make a fake warning feel legitimate.

That means the best defense is no longer trying to recognize every new scam script. It is creating one simple habit: Never make an important decision during an unexpected call, text or email. Hang up, verify the claim independently and involve someone you trust if anything feels off. A scammer needs urgency to win. Taking away that urgency puts you back in control.

response.snippet:
## What Is the Medicare Annual Enrollment Period?

The Medicare Annual Enrollment Period, also called Medicare open enrollment, runs October 15 through December 7 every year per CMS. Every person with Medicare can use this window to review their health and drug coverage and make changes for the following year. Changes made during the Annual Enrollment Period take effect January 1, 2027.

This is the primary opportunity to adjust Medicare coverage. Missing the December 7 deadline means your current plan renews automatically. The Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, which runs January 1 through March 31, allows more limited changes for people already enrolled in Medicare Advantage but does not offer the full range of options available during the Annual Enrollment Period. [...] Medicare’s Annual Enrollment Period opens October 15, 2026, one week from today. For every person enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan or Medicare Part D prescription drug plan, that date marks the start of a 54-day window to review current coverage, compare 2027 options, and make changes that take effect January 1, 2027. The window closes December 7. After that, your plan renews automatically, and your next primary opportunity to make changes is October 2027. [...] Call  to speak with a licensed Medicare advisor before the December 7 deadline.

## Frequently Asked Questions: Medicare Open Enrollment 2026

When does Medicare open enrollment start in 2026? The Medicare Annual Enrollment Period runs October 15 through December 7, 2026. All changes made during this window take effect January 1, 2027.

Is Medicare open enrollment the same as AEP? Yes. The Medicare Annual Enrollment Period and Medicare open enrollment refer to the same period, October 15 through December 7 each year. Some plans and advisors also call it the Fall Open Enrollment Period. All refer to the same 54-day window when any person with Medicare can review and change their coverage.
